title: Home Decor Inspiration
excerpt: A calm home is built from a few good decisions rather than a long shopping list. A room-by-room guide to the pieces that carry a home, and the habits that keep it quiet.

content.text: A calm home is built from a few good decisions rather than a long shopping list. Most rooms are carried by four or five pieces — somewhere to sit, somewhere to put things, a little warm light, and something soft underfoot — and everything else is detail. This guide works through those decisions in the order they matter, with a few pieces to shop under each.
Start with the largest piece

Every room has one piece that sets its tone, and it is almost always the largest. In a living room that is the sofa; in a bedroom, the bed. Choose it first, choose it slowly, and let the rest of the room arrange itself around it. A piece chosen for the room rather than for the season will still look right in ten years, while a fashionable one rarely lasts three.

Think about how the room is actually used rather than how it might photograph — how many people sit down on an ordinary evening, and where the light falls. Measure the wall before you fall in love with anything, leave room to walk around it, and let the room decide the shape rather than the trend.
Add a chair you actually want to sit in

A single good chair does more for a home than three ordinary ones. It fills the corner a sofa cannot reach, gives a bedroom somewhere to sit while you dress, and turns an unused corner into a place to read. Comfort is the whole point of it, so let that lead — a chair you are glad to sit in for an hour is worth more than one that only looks the part.
Place it where it will earn its keep: beside a window, near a lamp, or angled toward the rest of the seating so the room reads as arranged for company rather than pushed against the walls.
Give the clutter somewhere to go

Nothing unsettles a room faster than things with nowhere to live. One closed piece in each main room will hold most of it out of sight, and its top doubles as a surface for a lamp and one object you like. What it swallows changes from room to room — clothes, cables, keys and post — but the job is the same.
Keep that surface nearly bare. A cleared top is what makes a room read as calm rather than merely tidy.
Light it low and warm

A single bright ceiling light flattens a room and tires the eyes. Build the light up instead from lower, warmer sources — a floor lamp beside the seating, a soft glow in a corner — and the same room can serve a bright morning and a low-lit evening.
Warm-toned bulbs flatter a room and the people in it; cool white makes a home feel like an office. Where you can, add a dimmer and let the light drop as the day does.
Ground every room underfoot

A rug warms a hard floor, softens the sound of a busy room, and quietly draws a line around the furniture that sits on it. Size it generously: in a seating area the front legs of the sofa and chairs should rest on it, and a rug that is too small makes the whole room feel smaller.

Think about the room before anything else: a floor that takes daily traffic asks something different from a quiet corner, and how easily a rug cleans will matter more over the years than how it looks on the day it arrives.
Let one corner be green

A room with something growing in it reads as looked after in a way that furniture alone never manages. One larger plant usually does more than a scattering of small ones, and the corner that furniture leaves awkward is generally where it belongs.

Where the daylight never reaches, or the watering never quite happens, a faux tree holds the same shape and weight in the room and asks nothing of you. It is worth being honest with yourself about which of the two you will actually keep.
Dress the windows
Curtains do more than cover the glass. Cloth at a window absorbs sound, takes the hard edge off daylight, and brings in the one large soft surface a room full of hard ones is missing.

Hang the pole higher and wider than the frame, so the fabric sits clear of the glass when it is drawn back. The window looks taller for it, and none of the light you were trying to let in gets blocked.
Hang one mirror
A mirror is the cheapest way to change how much light a room has. Facing a window it hands the daylight back into the room; on a wall the sun never reaches, it opens a view where there was none.
One is usually enough. Hang it where it reflects something worth seeing — a window, a lamp, the green corner — rather than the back of a door.
Hold the palette to three quiet tones

Most calm homes run on three related tones: a pale base, a mid-tone, and one deeper shade to ground the room. Repeat each of them two or three times across the space — in the seating, the floor, a cushion — and the palette reads as considered rather than accidental.
Lean warm rather than cool. Oat, sand, clay and greige flatter almost any light, while cold greys can leave a room feeling unfinished on a dull day.
Let texture do the work colour usually does

When the palette is quiet, texture is what stops a room from feeling flat. Wood, stone, ceramic and cloth all read differently even in the same tone, and a room carrying three or four of them feels rich without ever raising its voice. Mix soft against hard, matte against smooth, and the depth arrives without any noise.
Buy slowly, and leave space

There is no rush to finish a room. Buying one considered piece at a time gives a home the collected feeling that a single delivery never does, and it leaves room to change your mind. Leave a clear stretch of floor, an empty end of a shelf, a bare patch of wall — the pauses are what let a home breathe.

title: Living Room Inspiration
excerpt: The living room holds more furniture and more daily use than any other space. A guide to the sofa, the seating around it, the light, the surfaces and the floor — and how to make them work together.

content.text: A living room brings together more furniture and more daily use than any other space in a home, so it rewards a little planning. The reliable approach is to start with the largest pieces and work down to the details — once the big things are settled, the smaller choices become easy and forgiving. Here is a way to think through each part, with a few pieces to shop under each.
Begin with the sofa

The sofa is the largest and most used seat in the room, so it deserves the most thought and most of the budget. Think about how many people you need to seat on an ordinary evening rather than at a party, and measure the wall before you fall in love with anything.

Let the room decide the shape: a long wall asks for something different from a square room with a corner to fill, and a piece that fits the space will always look calmer than one that fights it. Whatever you choose, pick something you are happy to live with rather than something you will be careful around.
Add a chair for the corner a sofa cannot reach

One or two chairs finish a living room and give it somewhere else to sit. Tucked into the corner a sofa cannot reach, a single armchair adds a seat without adding bulk, and it gives that part of the room a reason to exist.
Angle the chairs slightly toward the sofa rather than lining everything against the walls. A room arranged for conversation feels welcoming even when it is empty.
Light the room in layers

A single overhead light rarely does a living room justice. A mix of sources — a floor lamp beside the seating, a lower light in a corner — lets you set the mood for reading, relaxing or having people over, and keeps the evening from feeling like an office.

The most useful light falls where you actually sit rather than in the middle of the ceiling. A lamp beside the seating puts a warm pool where you read, and a warm bulb keeps the evening soft long after the daylight has gone.
Give the room one piece that hides things

A living room collects remote controls, chargers, papers and everything else the day leaves behind. One closed piece handles most of it, and it earns its keep twice over — hiding the clutter below and giving you a surface above.
Keep its top clear apart from a lamp, a tray, and one object you like, and the whole room stays calm even when the drawers are full.
Anchor the seating with a rug

A rug is what turns a group of furniture into a room. Size it so the front legs of the sofa and the chairs rest on it, and the whole seating area reads as one considered zone. A rug that is too small does the opposite, leaving the furniture adrift.

A living room floor takes more traffic than any other in the house, so how a rug cleans matters as much as how it looks. The one you can lift and wash without a second thought is the one you will still be glad of in two years.
Give one corner something green

Furniture on its own rarely makes a living room feel finished; something growing usually does. A single tall plant reads better than several small ones dotted about, and it earns the corner that seating tends to leave empty.
If the light in that corner is poor, or plants have never lasted long in your care, a faux tree keeps the same presence without the guilt of another one dying quietly behind the sofa.
Soften the window

A bare window leaves a living room sounding louder and feeling colder than it really is. Cloth at the glass absorbs the echo, filters the light coming through, and gives the eye somewhere gentle to land at the edge of the room.

Set the pole above and beyond the frame so the curtains clear the glass when open, and let them fall close to the floor. A curtain that stops short always looks as though it was cut for a different room.
Put a mirror where the light is short
Where a wall gets no daylight of its own, a mirror borrows some from the window opposite and gives it back to the room. It is the one piece that makes a space feel larger without taking any of it up.
Keep it to one. A wall of mirrors starts to read as a corridor rather than a room, and the trick stops working the moment it is repeated.
Layer the textiles

Cushions and throws are the easiest way to add warmth, and the easiest thing to change when a room starts to feel tired. Layer a few weaves rather than matching everything exactly — something smooth beside something with a bit of grain, one folded loosely over an arm — and the seating starts to invite you in rather than simply be looked at.
Keep the palette calm and repeat it

Hold the room to three related tones and repeat each one at least twice: the sofa and a cushion, the rug and a throw, a wood surface and a frame. Repetition is what makes a palette look deliberate rather than collected by accident.
Leave a little space empty
The instinct in a living room is to fill it; resist it. A clear stretch of floor, a bare patch of wall, an end table with nothing on it — these pauses are what make a busy room feel restful.

title: Bedroom Inspiration
excerpt: The one room with a single job: rest. A guide to a calm bedroom — the bed, the bedding, storage that clears the floor, somewhere to sit, soft light and what goes underfoot.

content.text: A bedroom has one real job — rest — and the calmest ones are built around that single idea. Keep the palette quiet, the surfaces clear and the light low, and the room does the rest. Here is a way to think it through, part by part.
Spend where your body spends the night

A simple, low bed frame matters far more than anything decorative. Centre it on the calmest wall, leave enough room to walk on either side, and let it anchor everything else in the room. Low frames keep the sightlines open, so the room reads as calm rather than crowded.
Beyond the frame, put the money into the mattress and the bedding rather than the headboard. They are what you actually feel.
Dress the bed

Bedding deserves more attention than almost anything else in the room, and it is the easiest thing to change when it stops working. Layer a lighter cover with a heavier throw at the foot, and the bed can be adjusted through the seasons rather than replaced.
Keep the bedding within your palette. A bed that recedes into the room is far more restful than one that shouts from the doorway.
Let one chest keep the room clear
Nothing unsettles a bedroom faster than clothes and clutter on show. One closed piece gives everything a place to disappear, and its top doubles as a surface for a lamp and a small tray.
Whatever you choose, leave its top almost empty. Clear surfaces are what make a bedroom feel like somewhere to rest rather than another room to tidy.
Keep one surface within reach of the bed

Whatever stands beside the bed ends up the busiest surface in the room — the lamp, the book, the glass of water, the phone you would rather not sleep next to. A drawer below takes most of that out of sight.
Where there is room on both sides of the bed, two of the same piece settles the room more than two unrelated ones. Where there is not, one is plenty.
Give yourself somewhere to sit

A bedroom is softened by a single chair — somewhere to sit while you dress, or read a few pages before sleep. One in the corner is enough, and it stops the bed from having to serve as the room's only seat.
Keep it clear. The danger of a bedroom chair is that it quietly becomes a pile of clothes.
Find room for a mirror you can see all of

A bedroom is where clothes get chosen, and choosing them from the waist up is guesswork. One mirror you can see the whole of settles that question every morning, and it does the same favour with light that any mirror does.

Leaning is easier than hanging and reads less formally, as long as the base sits secure against the wall. Place it where it catches the window rather than a blank stretch of wall, and it hands the daylight back into the room.
Keep the light low and warm

Bedrooms are for winding down, so save the overhead light for cleaning and let warm, low lamps take over in the evening. Light beside the bed, or one soft source in a reading corner, is all a bedroom really needs.
Warm bulbs settle the body for sleep; cool white keeps it alert. If you read in bed, put the light behind the shoulder so it falls on the page rather than into your eyes.
Soften the first step of the morning

A rug is the first thing your feet meet each day, so comfort is worth thinking about here more than anywhere else in the house. Lay it so it reaches out from under the bed on the sides you actually get out of.
Whatever you choose, let it settle quietly with the rest of the room rather than announce itself.
Cover the window properly

A bedroom asks more of its curtains than any other room, because they have to hold back the morning as well as dress the wall. It is the one place where how well they close matters more than how they look.
Hang the pole high and wide so the cloth clears the glass when open, and let it fall close to the floor. Tied back through the day, the same curtains give the light somewhere to come in.
Hold the palette quiet

Warm neutrals — oat, sand, clay, greige — flatter a bedroom in both morning light and lamplight, where colder tones can leave it looking unfinished. Let the largest surfaces carry the quietest of them, and save any depth for the smaller pieces, which are also the easiest to change when you tire of them.
Clear the surfaces each night

The best bedroom habit costs nothing: clear the bedside and the top of the chest before you sleep. A lamp, a book and one small object is plenty, and waking to a calm room is worth the two minutes it takes.
The one thing worth putting back is a clock. Leaving the phone to charge in another room is far easier when something else is doing the waking.

title: Dining Room Inspiration
excerpt: A few things done well — a table you gather around, chairs that make people linger, light that flatters the food, and a rug that holds it all together.

content.text: A dining room needs only a few things done well: a table you are happy to gather around, chairs that make people want to linger, and light that flatters the food and the faces around it. Get those right and every smaller choice becomes forgiving. Here is how to think it through.
Buy the most honest table you can

Solid, simple, and a touch larger than you think you need — that is the whole brief. Real timber takes a scratch as character rather than damage, and a table that carries a few marks is far more welcoming than one everyone is careful around.
Round and oval shapes let you seat an extra guest without anyone catching a corner. Whatever the shape, leave the top mostly bare between meals and let it be the quiet centre of the room.
Choose chairs you can sit in for two hours
Comfort matters more than matching. Chairs you can settle into are what turn a quick supper into an evening, and a little padding or a soft seat pad against a hard top makes all the difference.
They need not match the table. A gentle contrast — pale wood against a darker surface, a softer seat against a solid frame — usually reads as more considered than a matching set bought together.
Hang the light low and keep it warm

Light over a dining table should pool on the surface rather than glare into eyes, so hang it lower than feels natural — roughly at head height when standing. Keep the bulbs warm so they flatter the food and the company.

A dimmer earns its place here more than in any other room: the same light can serve a bright breakfast and a slow, low evening. A few candles set low along the table finish it, and make an ordinary meal feel considered.
Lay a rug that fits the table properly

A rug under the table softens the room and catches the scrape of chairs on a hard floor. The one rule that matters is size: measure the table with the chairs pulled out, then choose a rug a little larger, so nobody catches an edge when they sit down.
Dining rooms see the odd spill, so how easily a rug cleans matters here, as does whether chairs move over it comfortably. Those two questions count for more in this room than in any other.
Keep one surface for serving

A sideboard or low console along one wall holds what the table cannot and gives you somewhere to serve from, so the table itself can stay clear. Keep it against the wall so it never eats into the space around the chairs, and keep its top to one or two things.
Leave room to pull the chairs out

Allow a clear arm's length behind each chair so people can sit and rise without a struggle, and keep a clear path from the door to the seats. It is the most common thing to get wrong in a dining room and the easiest to plan for.
Repeat one wood and one soft material

A dining room settles when its materials agree. Choose a single wood tone and repeat it across the table, a chair frame and a serving board, then let one soft material — linen napkins, a runner, a seat pad — appear two or three times. Repetition is what makes the room feel designed rather than assembled.
Style the table with restraint

Between meals, a wooden board, a low bowl of whatever fruit is in season, and one simple vase are enough. A table left mostly clear is more inviting than one dressed for a photograph, and it is ready for the next meal without a tidy-up.
